I4.quote: Searched text, captions, EDX table and page images for a surface area of any sample; none found. Section 2.3 gives only a 'Typical' open bound ('≥ 10 m2/gm') and says the BET condition 'is not satisfied here'.

I5.quote: Carbons are being widely investigated as hydrogen storage material owing to their light weight, fast hydrogen adsorption kinetics and cost effectiveness.

notes: I4 is borderline. The only surface-area passage is main, p. 3, Section 2.3: 'Typical BET surface area found by nitrogen adsorption at the surface is ≥ 10 m2/gm' (page image confirms '≥'), followed by 'the required condition for surface area through nitrogen BET technique is not satisfied here. In view of this, the low surface area observed in the present investigation can be understood.' I judged I4 not met because no sample is given a surface-area value: the figure is stated as typical, is an open lower bound that contradicts the authors' own 'low surface area', and the authors frame the measurement as an attempt whose BET precondition fails. A reader who accepts a method-identified bound tied to the present material ('found', 'observed in the present investigation') as a reported area would code I4 met and the paper eligible; I1, I2, I3 and I5 are met and no other code applies. Other observations: the record is an arXiv preprint with original data, treated as primary; not retracted; no duplicate-data statement. Uptake measured on a Sieverts PCI unit at 30 °C and 77 K, 30 and 70 atm, as uptake-vs-time curves (Fig. 1a, 1b) plus a 30 °C PCI isotherm to about 41 atm (Fig. 1c). The Fig. 1(b) legend appears to swap the 30 and 70 atm labels relative to the text, and Section 3.4 (p. 5) gives 3.00 wt.% at 30 atm, 77 K where Section 3.1 gives 3.50 wt.%. Sorbent is carbonized coconut endosperm (350 °C, N2) with native KCl and Mg; EDX C 70.60 wt%.
